etymology: From the Saxon wearp, from weorpan, “to throw or cast” — the threads cast lengthwise upon the loom and stretched taut between the beams before ever a shuttle crosses them.
biblical_def: The warp is the lengthwise thread of the loom: the set of strands strung upon the beams, held in tension, and fixed in place before the weaving begins. It is not the pattern that the eye admires; it is the skeleton the pattern hangs upon. Take the warp away and there is no cloth, only a heap of yarn. Scripture uses the word almost wholly in one place, and that place is a chapter about defilement. In the law of the leprosy of garments the priest is charged to examine not merely the surface of the cloth but its structure: “Whether it be in the warp, or woof; of linen, or of woollen; whether in a skin, or in any thing made of skin” (Lev 13:48). The plague is traced into the very threads. If it has entered the warp, no scouring of the face of the garment will do; the whole must be burnt (Lev 13:52). That is the doctrine the loom is made to teach. Sin in Scripture is never a stain lying upon an otherwise sound nature; it has gone down into the lengthwise threads of the man, into the frame upon which every thought and word and work is woven. Total depravity is warp-depravity. And this is why the remedy is not laundering but a new creation — not a garment washed, but a garment given, the imputed righteousness of Christ, woven whole from above.
webster_summary: The threads extended lengthwise in the loom, crossed by the woof; hence the foundation-threads of any woven cloth.
webster_full: WARP, n. [Sax. wearp, from weorpan, to cast or throw.] In manufactures, the threads which are extended lengthwise in the loom, and crossed by the woof.
To warp, in the verbal sense, is to turn or twist out of shape by unequal shrinking — whence the figurative use for a mind turned aside from rectitude.
The warp is strung and stretched before weaving begins; the woof is thrown across it by the shuttle.
Scripture employs the term in the law of leprosy in garments, distinguishing the plague in the warp from the plague in the woof (Lev 13:48-59).
Figuratively, the ground-work or substance of any thing; that upon which the rest is wrought.
scriptures: Whether it be in the warp, or woof; of linen, or of woollen; whether in a skin, or in any thing made of skin;
And if the plague be greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it is a plague of leprosy, and shall be shewed unto the priest:
He shall therefore burn that garment, whether warp or woof, in woollen or in linen, or any thing of skin, wherein the plague is: for it is a fretting leprosy; it shall be burnt in the fire.
This is the law of the plague of leprosy in a garment of woollen or linen, either in the warp, or woof, or any thing of skins, to pronounce it clean, or to pronounce it unclean.
corruption_summary: The garment law of Lev 13 is emptied of doctrine and re-labelled an ancient sanitation code — mildew management for a pre-scientific people — which silences everything the warp was meant to preach.
corruption_paragraphs: The common modern handling of Lev 13 is to reduce it to public health: a bronze-age quarantine manual for mould in cloth, interesting to the antiquarian, binding on no one, teaching nothing. The reduction is tidy and it is false, and the text itself refutes it. A sanitation officer does not need a priest; this examination is committed to the priest, at the door of the tabernacle, and its verdict is not safe or unsafe but clean or unclean — a standing before God, not a hazard to the lungs. A sanitation code does not require a garment to be brought out and burnt when a washing would serve, nor does it call the spot a fretting leprosy, borrowing the vocabulary of the plague in human flesh from the chapter’s first half. The law is deliberately teaching by analogy: what leprosy is in the body, this is in the cloth, and both are parables of what sin is in the sinner. Strip the doctrine out and you keep the hygiene and lose the gospel, which is precisely the trade the rationalist reading proposes.

Recover the lesson the warp was strung to teach. First, that sin penetrates: it does not sit on the surface of a nature otherwise sound but runs in the lengthwise threads, so that the whole man — mind, will, affections — is implicated. Second, that God’s inspection is total. The priest looks past the face of the cloth into its structure, and the LORD searches the heart and tries the reins. Third, that where the plague is in the warp the sentence is fire, and no laundering will avert it — which is why the sinner’s hope has never been improvement. Christ does not scour the old garment; He clothes us in another. Read Lev 13 as the ceremonial shadow it is, and it drives you to the same place Isaiah’s crimson does: not to the washtub, but to the Lamb.
roots_summary: The lengthwise threads of the loom — the frame of the cloth; in Lev 13 the depth into which the plague may run.
roots_lines: Warp — Saxon wearp, from weorpan, to cast or throw upon the beams.
Hebrew shethi, the set thread, from a root meaning to set or place (Lev 13:48).
Always paired in Scripture with woof ('erebh), the thread thrown across it.
Nine occurrences, all within the garment-leprosy law of Lev 13:48-59.
The priest, not the launderer, pronounces upon it: clean or unclean before God.
usage: Sin is not a stain on the cloth but a plague in the warp — hence a new garment, not a washing.
The priest examined the structure, not the surface: God tries the frame of a man, not his appearance.
Where the plague was in the warp, fire was the sentence — a shadow of the judgment reformation cannot avert.

etymology: From the Saxon wefan, “to weave,” the same root that yields web and weft — the thread thrown crosswise by the shuttle over and under the standing warp.
biblical_def: The woof is the crosswise thread, carried by the shuttle over and under the warp until the cloth is filled and closed. Where the warp is the frame, the woof is the filling: the warp is set once and holds still, the woof travels and returns and travels again, and between them the garment comes to be. Scripture names the woof only in the law of the leprosy of garments, where the priest must judge the plague “either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin” (Lev 13:51). The pairing is the point. God does not permit the examination to stop at one thread. A man may be sound in the standing frame of his profession and rotten in the daily crossing threads of his conduct, or orderly in his habits and corrupt in the fixed principles beneath them; the law will have both searched. Nor is the verdict left to the owner of the coat: the garment is shewed unto the priest, shut up seven days, looked upon again, and either washed a second time and pronounced clean (Lev 13:58) or burnt with fire (Lev 13:57). Here is the pattern of true self-examination — patient, repeated, submitted to God’s appointed word rather than to our own quick verdict, and content with no cleanness but the cleanness He pronounces.
webster_summary: The threads that cross the warp in weaving; the weft or filling of a woven cloth.
webster_full: WOOF, n. [Sax. wefan, to weave.] The threads that cross the warp in weaving; the weft.
Hence, texture; cloth; that which is woven.
The woof is thrown by the shuttle; the warp lies extended and receives it.
The term occurs in Scripture only in the law concerning the plague of leprosy in a garment (Lev 13:48-59).
The same Saxon root yields web, weft, and weave.
scriptures: And he shall look on the plague on the seventh day: if the plague be spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in a skin, or in any work that is made of skin; the plague is a fretting leprosy; it is unclean.
And if the priest shall look, and, behold, the plague be not spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin;
And if it appear still in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it is a spreading plague: thou shalt burn that wherein the plague is with fire.
And the garment, either warp, or woof, or whatsoever thing of skin it be, which thou shalt wash, if the plague be departed from them, then it shall be washed the second time, and shall be clean.
corruption_summary: No party has redefined the woof; the loss is simply that a working word has become an idiom — “the warp and woof of” — while the Levitical chapter that gave it weight goes unread.
corruption_paragraphs: What has happened to the woof is not redefinition but forgetfulness. The phrase warp and woof survives in ordinary speech as a way of saying the very fabric of a thing, and men use it who have never stood at a loom and never read Lev 13. The image keeps its force precisely because everyone senses that warp and woof means all the way through, which is the sense the priest was given to test. So the idiom is a fossil of a doctrine: it remembers that some faults are structural while others are superficial, and that the difference matters. The word does no harm in its modern dress; it is simply doing less work than it was given.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the discipline of the seventh-day look. The priest did not pronounce at once; he shut the garment up, looked again after seven days, and judged by whether the plague had spread. That is the God-given shape of self-examination, and it corrects two errors at a stroke. It corrects the hasty despair that condemns itself the moment a spot appears, and it corrects the hasty presumption that pronounces itself clean before the second washing. Try yourself in both threads — the fixed principles you hold and the daily crossings of your conduct — and let the verdict be God’s, given by His word, not your own mood. “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith” is the same law brought forward, and the same patience is required of it.
roots_summary: The crosswise thread thrown by the shuttle; with the warp, the whole substance of the cloth under the priest’s eye.
roots_lines: Woof — Saxon wefan, to weave; cognate with web and weft.
Hebrew 'erebh, from a root meaning to interweave or mix in.
Never appears in Scripture apart from warp; the two are always judged together.
Confined to Lev 13:48-59, the law of leprosy in a garment.
The seventh-day re-examination governs the verdict: spread means unclean; departed means washed again and clean.
usage: Warp and woof together: God searches the fixed principles and the daily conduct alike.
The seventh-day look forbids both hasty despair and hasty self-acquittal.
Cleanness is pronounced by the priest, not claimed by the owner of the garment.

etymology: From the Saxon wull, akin to the Latin vellus, a fleece — the soft crimped fibre shorn from the sheep, the plainest clothing of the plainest people, and in Scripture the standing figure of whiteness.
biblical_def: Wool is the fleece of the sheep, shorn, washed, carded, and spun. It is the poor man’s warmth and the shepherd’s wage, the first fruit of the flock and the commonest cloth in Israel. Scripture makes three great uses of it. First, it is the emblem of pardon: “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool” (Isa 1:18). The Lord does not say the scarlet will be dulled or covered; He says it shall be as wool, which is white not by bleaching but by nature, as it comes from the beast. That is justification, not reformation. Second, wool is the emblem of the Ancient of days, whose hair is “like the pure wool” (Dan 7:9), and of the glorified Christ, whose head and hairs were white like wool (Rev 1:14) — eternity and spotless purity in one image. Third, wool is fenced by law. It may not be woven with linen in one garment (Deu 22:11), and the ministering priests of Ezekiel’s temple wear linen only, for “no wool shall come upon them” where they sweat and serve. The virtuous woman seeks wool and flax and works willingly with her hands (Pro 31:13); Gideon laid a fleece of wool upon the floor and asked a sign.
webster_summary: The soft curled hair or fleece of sheep and like animals; in Scripture the emblem of whiteness, of pardon, and of the Ancient of days.
webster_full: WOOL, n. [Sax. wull; L. vellus, a fleece.] That soft species of hair which grows on sheep and some other animals, remarkable for its crimped fibre, which fits it for spinning and felting.
It is distinguished from hair by its curl and its readiness to mat and take the dye.
Short, curled hair on the head, as in the phrase “hair like the pure wool” (Dan 7:9).
The Mosaic law forbade the wearing of a garment of woollen and linen together (Deu 22:11; Lev 19:19).
Wool and flax are named together as the staple materials of household industry (Pro 31:13; Hos 2:9).
scriptures: Isa 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
Thou shalt not wear a garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together.
Dan 7:9

I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool: his throne was like the fiery flame, and his wheels as burning fire.
Jdg 6:37

Behold, I will put a fleece of wool in the floor; and if the dew be on the fleece only, and it be dry upon all the earth beside, then shall I know that thou wilt save Israel by mine hand, as thou hast said.
corruption_summary: Gideon’s fleece has been turned into a method. “Putting out a fleece” is now taught as an ordinary way to get guidance from God, and the prosperity preachers make it a lever for extracting promised returns.
corruption_paragraphs: Jdg 6:37 has been lifted out of its narrative and made a technique. Believers are taught to “put out a fleece” — to name a sign, set a condition, and read the outcome as God’s voice — and in the prosperity teaching the fleece becomes frankly transactional: a sum given, a seed sown, with a specified return demanded of God in exchange. Both misuse the text. Gideon was not seeking guidance; he had already been told plainly, twice, what the LORD would do. He was doubting a word already spoken, and he knew it, for he says, “Let not thine anger be hot against me.” God condescended to a weak and fearful man, as He often does, but condescension to weakness is not the institution of a method. Nor is the fleece a lever. The God who answered Gideon is not a mechanism to be operated by anyone who repeats the motions, and the promise attached to the modern fleece — give this, receive that — is not found in Judges or anywhere else. We are not left to signs. We have the Scriptures, the counsel of the church, the ordinary providence of God, and prayer for wisdom which He gives liberally and upbraideth not.

Recover instead what wool was chiefly given to preach. Isa 1:18 is the high use, and it is a courtroom scene, not a laundry. The LORD summons a rebellious people to reason with Him, and He does not propose that they scrub the scarlet out; He declares what He will make of it. Scarlet and crimson were the fastest dyes known — twice-dipped, deliberately permanent, the very colours chosen because they would not wash out. That is the choice of the figure: sin at its most ineradicable, set against a whiteness that is not achieved but given, the native whiteness of the fleece as it leaves the sheep. And the whiteness has a cost, for the fleece comes off a lamb. So the wool of Isa 1:18 and the Lamb of Joh 1:29 are the same doctrine: righteousness imputed, not attained; a garment received, not laundered.
roots_summary: The shorn fleece of the sheep — the commonest cloth in Israel and the Bible’s standing emblem of a whiteness that is given, not achieved.
roots_lines: Wool — Saxon wull; compare Latin vellus, a fleece.
Hebrew tsemer, wool; Greek erion (Heb 9:19; Rev 1:14).
Isa 1:18 sets it against scarlet and crimson — the two fastest dyes of the ancient world.
Dan 7:9 and Rev 1:14 give the same white-wool hair to the Ancient of days and to the risen Christ.
Forbidden to be mingled with linen in one garment (Deu 22:11) and excluded from the ministering priest’s dress (Eze 44:17).
usage: As wool, not bleached wool: Isa 1:18 promises a whiteness native to the fleece, which is imputation, not reform.
Scarlet and crimson were chosen because they never wash out — that is the measure of the mercy.
Gideon’s fleece was condescension to a fearful man, never a method for prying guidance out of God.

etymology: Through the Saxon seolc from the Latin sericum, the cloth of the Seres, the far eastern people from whom the fibre came — a name that carried its own distance and cost in it.
biblical_def: Silk is the fine lustrous thread reeled from the cocoon and woven into the costliest of cloths, brought into Israel from far countries and priced accordingly. In the Authorized Version it appears only a handful of times, and every appearance is loaded. Twice it is the LORD’s own gift to His bride: in Ezekiel’s parable Jerusalem is the abandoned infant whom God washes, clothes, and adorns — “I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk” (Eze 16:10), until she was “exceeding beautiful” and prospered into a kingdom (Eze 16:13). Every thread of her splendour was given her. Once it is the honourable dress of a diligent woman: the virtuous wife of Pro 31, whose hands seek wool and flax and whose clothing is silk and purple — the cloth is not condemned, for it is the fruit of her own industry and the credit of her husband in the gates. And once it lies in the cargo of a doomed city: “the merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stones, and of pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet” (Rev 18:12), which no man buyeth any more. So silk stands between two poles. Received as God’s gift it clothes a bride; loved for itself it becomes the freight of Babylon.
webster_summary: The fine glossy thread spun by the silkworm, and the costly cloth woven of it; in Scripture a gift bestowed upon the bride and a staple of Babylon’s merchandise.
webster_full: SILK, n. [Sax. seolc; L. sericum, from Seres, the eastern people who first furnished it.] The fine soft thread produced by the silkworm, and the cloth manufactured from it.
It is remarkable for lustre, strength, and lightness, and has always been ranked among the most costly of stuffs.
Anciently brought overland from the east at great charge, whence its use marked royalty and wealth.
In Scripture the clothing bestowed upon Jerusalem in the parable of Eze 16, and part of the merchandise of Babylon (Rev 18:12).
Also the dress of the virtuous woman of Pro 31:22, whose clothing is silk and purple.
scriptures: I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers' skin, and I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk.
But thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown, and pouredst out thy fornications on every one that passed by; his it was.
She maketh herself coverings of tapestry; her clothing is silk and purple.

The merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stones, and of pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood, and all manner vessels of ivory, and all manner vessels of most precious wood, and of brass, and iron, and marble,
corruption_summary: Silk is claimed as proof-text by two opposite errors: the prosperity preacher who reads Pro 31:22 as a mandate for luxury, and the ascetic who reads Rev 18:12 as a ban on any fine thing at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching seizes on Eze 16 and Pro 31 and argues that God clothes His people in silk, therefore fine living is the birthright of faith and want is the mark of unbelief. The argument dies on the next verses. Ezekiel’s silk is prologue to the most terrible indictment in the prophets: “thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown” (Eze 16:15). The gift became the occasion of the sin, because she began to read it as a wage rather than a mercy, and the chapter ends in the stripping of everything the opening bestowed. That is not a promise of luxury; it is a warning about what luxury does to a heart that forgets who gave it. At the other pole stands the reflex that treats any costly thing as sin in itself, and here Pro 31:22 stands in the way — the woman whose clothing is silk and purple is the woman the chapter praises, whose hands hold the distaff, whose candle goeth not out by night, and who stretcheth out her hand to the poor. Scripture never made poverty a virtue nor wealth a proof.

The dividing line runs through Rev 18. Babylon’s sin was not that silk existed in her warehouses but that her whole life was freight — buying and selling, and the souls of men reckoned as the last item on the manifest. When the city falls, the merchants weep, and they weep for their trade, not for the dead. So the question the word puts to us is never simply what we wear but what we are holding. Receive fine things as Ezekiel’s foundling received hers — as sheer gift to one who had nothing and deserved less — and they will not ruin you. Trust in them, price your standing by them, spend your years accumulating them, and you are already in the cargo lists of a city that is coming down in one hour.
roots_summary: The costliest imported cloth of the ancient world — in Scripture the bride’s bestowed adorning and Babylon’s unsellable freight.
roots_lines: Silk — Saxon seolc, Latin sericum, the cloth of the Seres.
Hebrew meshi, a costly drawn-out stuff (Eze 16:10, 13); Greek sirikon (Rev 18:12).
Every Old Testament use is bestowed clothing — given, not earned.
Eze 16 gives it and Eze 16:39 strips it away again when the bride turns harlot.
In Rev 18:12 it stands third in Babylon’s manifest, which ends with “slaves, and souls of men.”
usage: Ezekiel’s silk was a gift to a foundling — every thread of it, and she forgot the giver.
Pro 31 praises a woman clothed in silk and purple: Scripture makes poverty no virtue and wealth no proof.
Babylon’s sin was not owning silk but being freight — her manifest ends with the souls of men.

etymology: From the Saxon thraed, from thrawan, “to twist” — fibres twisted together into a single line; the smallest unit of every woven thing, and the least valuable object a man could name.
biblical_def: A thread is a twisted line of fibre — the smallest thing on the loom, and in Scripture the standing measure of what is negligible. Abram swears to the king of Sodom that he will not take so much as a thread or a shoelatchet from him, lest the king should say he had made Abram rich (Gen 14:23): the least thread of Sodom’s wealth was too much for a man whose portion was God. Samson snapped new ropes from off his arms “like a thread” (Jdg 16:12), the strongest cord reckoned as nothing to the Spirit’s strength. The Song praises a bride whose lips are “like a thread of scarlet” (Son 4:3), fine and vivid together. But the great thread of the Bible hangs in a window in Jericho. The spies charge Rahab: “thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by” (Jos 2:18), and every soul she gathers under that roof lives while the city falls. She bound it at once, before the armies came, while the walls still stood and there was nothing to see (Jos 2:21). The thread saved nobody by its strength. It saved by being the appointed sign, the same red mark as the blood on the doorposts — a token of covenant, hung in faith, honoured by God.
webster_summary: A small line of twisted fibre; hence the least or slenderest thing; in Scripture the scarlet token of Rahab’s deliverance.
webster_full: THREAD, n. [Sax. thraed, from thrawan, to twist.] A small line of fibres twisted together, of flax, wool, cotton, or silk, used in sewing and weaving.
Hence, any thing very slender or of small value: “from a thread even to a shoelatchet” (Gen 14:23).
Figuratively, the continuous course of a discourse or narration — the thread of an argument.
In Jos 2:18 the scarlet thread bound in Rahab’s window, the token of her house’s preservation.
A threefold cord, of threads twisted together, is not quickly broken (Ecc 4:12).
scriptures: Jos 2:18

Behold, when we come into the land, thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by: and thou shalt bring thy father, and thy mother, and thy brethren, and all thy father's household, home unto thee.
Jos 2:21
And she said, According unto your words, so be it. And she sent them away, and they departed: and she bound the scarlet line in the window.

Delilah therefore took new ropes, and bound him therewith, and said unto him, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And there were liers in wait abiding in the chamber. And he brake them from off his arms like a thread.
Son 4:3
Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy speech is comely: thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate within thy locks.
corruption_summary: No modern movement contests the meaning of a thread; the loss is that Rahab’s scarlet line is read as a charming detail of a spy story rather than as the appointed token of covenant deliverance.
corruption_paragraphs: Rahab’s thread has suffered nothing worse than being made picturesque. Retold as adventure, the scarlet line becomes a clever signal — a marker so the soldiers would know which house to spare — and the whole weight of it drains away into logistics. But Scripture will not let it stay small. Rahab is named twice in the New Testament, once among the heroes of faith and once among those justified by works that proved faith real, and the God who reckoned her righteous set her in the line of David and of Christ Himself. The thread was not signage; it was the visible pledge of a sworn covenant, bound in the window by faith before there was any army in sight, and it is joined by every instinct of the type to the blood struck on the lintel in Egypt, where again a red mark on the outside of a house was the whole difference between the living and the dead.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the strength of a token is never in the token. A thread stops no soldier. A smear of lamb’s blood stops no destroyer. What saved Rahab’s household was the word of the men who swore to her and the God who stood behind their oath, and the thread was simply the appointed way of taking Him at His word. So it is with every sign God has given. Baptism does not wash the conscience and the Supper does not feed the soul by any power resident in water or bread; they are covenant tokens, and their whole value lies in the faithfulness of Him who appointed them. Bind the thread early, as Rahab did — while the walls still stand and nothing has begun to shake — and gather your household inside the house where the sign is hung.
roots_summary: The least thing on the loom — Abram’s measure of what he would not take, and Rahab’s scarlet token of deliverance.
roots_lines: Thread — Saxon thraed, from thrawan, to twist.
Hebrew chut, a line or thread (Jos 2:18; Ecc 4:12); tiqvah, a cord, in Jos 2:18’s “line.”
The proverbial name for the negligible: not a thread nor a shoelatchet (Gen 14:23).
Rahab’s scarlet thread joins the blood of the lintel (Exo 12:13) as a red token of covenant deliverance.
Son 4:3 uses it for fineness and vivid colour together in the praise of the bride.
usage: Abram would not take a thread of Sodom’s wealth — a man whose portion is God can afford to refuse.
Rahab bound the line while the walls still stood: faith hangs the token before the shaking begins.
The thread had no strength; the oath behind it had all the strength — which is how every covenant sign works.

etymology: From the Saxon deagan, “to colour,” from deag, a dye — to strike a colour into a fibre so that it becomes the fibre’s own and cannot be rinsed away.
biblical_def: To dye is to drive colour into a fibre until it is no longer a coating but a property of the thread. Scripture uses the word in three settings, and each turns on that permanence. In the tabernacle, the LORD calls for “rams' skins dyed red” (Exo 25:5) as a covering for the tent, laid beneath the badgers' skins where no worshipper could see them (Exo 26:14). The house of God was roofed in red, and the red was hidden — the blood-covering that shelters the holy place is not for display. In Ezekiel, dyed attire is the mark of seduction: the Chaldean princes portrayed upon the wall, girded and “exceeding in dyed attire upon their heads” (Eze 23:15), a splendour painted to be lusted after. And in Isaiah the dye is on the Conqueror Himself: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa 63:1). The answer comes back, “I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save,” and the chapter tells us what dyed those garments — He trod the winepress alone, and the blood of His enemies is sprinkled upon His raiment. The whole Bible’s colour theology stands in that image: red struck permanently into cloth, whether as covering, as temptation, or as the livery of judgment.
webster_summary: Stained or coloured by dye, so that the colour becomes proper to the fibre; in Scripture the red covering of the tabernacle and the stained garments of the Conqueror from Bozrah.
webster_full: DYED, pp. [Sax. deagan, to colour, from deag, a dye.] Stained; coloured; having a colour struck into the substance.
Distinguished from painting or staining the surface: the dye enters the fibre and becomes proper to it.
The fastest ancient dyes were the scarlet of the kermes insect and the purple of the murex, both prized for permanence.
Rams' skins dyed red formed the third covering of the tabernacle (Exo 25:5; 26:14; 36:19; 39:34).
Dyed attire, in Eze 23:15, denotes the coloured headdress of the Babylonian princes.
scriptures: Exo 25:5
And rams' skins dyed red, and badgers' skins, and shittim wood,
And thou shalt make a covering for the tent of rams' skins dyed red, and a covering above of badgers' skins.
Isa 63:1
Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.
Girded with girdles upon their loins, exceeding in dyed attire upon their heads, all of them princes to look to, after the manner of the Babylonians of Chaldea, the land of their nativity:
corruption_summary: No party is redefining the word; what is commonly lost is that Isa 63 is a judgment oracle, softened by preachers into a picture of the Saviour stained with His own blood at Calvary.
corruption_paragraphs: Isa 63:1-6 is regularly preached as a Passion text: the Man from Edom in dyed garments is taken for Christ crimsoned with His own wounds, and the winepress is read as the cross. The instinct is devout and the reading is wrong, and the passage says so in plain words. “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments.” Their blood. The dye is the blood of His enemies, not His own; the day is the day of vengeance in His heart; and Revelation takes up the same figure for the rider on the white horse who treads the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God. Softening it does not make Christ kinder, it makes Him smaller, and it robs the afflicted church of the very comfort the oracle was given to supply — that there is a day appointed when the Lamb rises as Judge and the account of Edom is settled by His own hand.

Hold the two dyed cloths together and the doctrine is whole. Under the tabernacle roof lay rams' skins dyed red, unseen by any worshipper, silently covering the house where God met His people — atonement made, and made out of sight, so that the man who came with his offering was sheltered by a red he never looked at. Over Edom comes the Conqueror in garments dyed with the blood of His foes. The same Christ is both coverings: red beneath for those who are His, red upon Him against those who are not. There is no third option and no neutral ground, for every man is either under the covering or in front of the winepress. That is why the ram’s skin was dyed and not merely painted: what God does in atonement and in judgment alike goes all the way into the fibre and never washes out.
roots_summary: Colour struck permanently into the fibre — the hidden red roof of the tabernacle and the stained garments of the Conqueror from Bozrah.
roots_lines: Dyed — Saxon deagan, to colour; deag, a dye.
Hebrew 'adam, to be red, in the phrase “rams' skins dyed red” (me'oddamim).
The tabernacle’s third covering, laid under the badgers' skins and seen by none (Exo 26:14).
Isa 63:1 — garments dyed from Bozrah in Edom, the blood being the enemies’ own (Isa 63:3).
Eze 23:15 — dyed attire as the painted splendour that drew Aholibah into idolatry.
usage: A dye enters the fibre; a paint sits on it — which is why Scripture chose dye for what cannot be undone.
The tabernacle was roofed in red that no worshipper ever saw: atonement made, not displayed.
Isa 63 is vengeance, not Calvary — the blood on those garments belongs to Edom.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s spelling of cloak, through Old French cloque, a bell — so named from the shape of the wide outer garment hanging bell-like from the shoulders; hence also the figure of anything spread over to hide what is beneath.
biblical_def: The cloke is the wide outer garment worn over the coat, the last covering a man had and often his bedding by night, which is why the law forbade keeping a poor man’s pledged garment past sundown. Our Lord takes it up in the Sermon on the Mount: “if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also” (Mat 5:40). The command is not that we care nothing for justice, but that a disciple will sooner be stripped than be litigious, and will not clutch the last covering when peace with a brother is the price. Paul, at the end of his life and cold in a Roman cell, sends for the cloke he left at Troas with Carpus (2Ti 4:13) — a plain reminder that the apostle who wrote of the third heaven still needed a coat in winter. But the word’s second use is the sharper one. A cloke covers, and therefore Scripture names it as the very figure of pretence: Christ says of those who heard Him and rejected Him, “now they have no cloke for their sin” (Joh 15:22); Paul denies ever using flattering words “as a cloke of covetousness” (1Th 2:5); and Peter warns the free man not to use his liberty “for a cloke of maliciousness” (1Pe 2:16). The garment men throw over sin is always someone else’s virtue.
webster_summary: A loose outer garment worn over the rest; hence, figuratively, any covering or pretext thrown over sin to hide it.
webster_full: CLOKE, n. [Old Fr. cloque, a bell, from the shape.] A loose outer garment worn over the other clothes, covering the whole person.
Hence, a cover; a pretext; a pretence; that which conceals a design or a fault.
In the law, the outer garment taken in pledge must be restored before sundown, being the poor man’s covering by night (Exo 22:26-27).
Christ commands the disciple sued for his coat to yield the cloke also (Mat 5:40; Luk 6:29).
Figurative in Joh 15:22, 1Th 2:5, and 1Pe 2:16 — a cloke for sin, for covetousness, for maliciousness.
scriptures: Mat 5:40
And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also.
If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin.
As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.
The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.
corruption_summary: The cloke is alive and thriving. What has changed is its fabric: sin is now covered with explanation — circumstance, upbringing, temperament, brain chemistry — and confession is treated as the unhealthy thing to be talked out of.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ’s verdict in Joh 15:22 is that light removes the covering: once He had come and spoken, the sin stood naked and no cloke could be found for it. Our age has answered by weaving new ones. The besetting sin is renamed a condition, the temper a wiring, the appetite an orientation, the cruelty a wound passed down; each account may hold some measure of truth about the occasion of the sin, and each becomes a cloke the moment it is offered in the place of confession. Scripture does not deny that men are shaped by what befalls them — it speaks constantly of the fathers’ sins, of affliction, of the frame that God remembers to be dust — but it never permits the shaping to become the excuse. David had every circumstance to plead and pleaded none of them: “against thee, thee only, have I sinned.” The reason is mercy, not severity. Nothing that is cloked can be forgiven, because nothing that is cloked is confessed, and “he that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13).

Peter names the most refined cloke of all: liberty. “As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness” — that is, taking the true doctrine that a Christian is free from the law’s condemnation and pulling it over conduct the law condemns. Paul’s version is flattery serving greed. In both cases the covering is not a lie but a truth misapplied, which is what makes it hard to strip off; the man is quoting sound doctrine while doing wickedness. The remedy is the one Christ Himself supplies. He does not merely tear the cloke away; He offers another garment in its place, the best robe brought out for the returning son. Confession is safe precisely because there is a covering that God Himself gives, and no man ever had to invent his own who was willing to wear Christ’s.
roots_summary: The wide outer garment — a poor man’s last covering, and Scripture’s standing figure for the pretext thrown over sin.
roots_lines: Cloke — the Authorized Version’s spelling of cloak; Old French cloque, a bell, from the garment’s shape.
Greek himation in Mat 5:40, the outer garment as against the chiton or coat.
Greek prophasis in Joh 15:22, 1Th 2:5, 1Pe 2:16 — a pretext, a thing put forward to cover.
Greek phelones in 2Ti 4:13, a traveller’s heavy cape left behind at Troas.
Isa 59:17 clothes the LORD Himself with zeal as a cloke — the one covering that hides nothing.
usage: Yield the cloke rather than the peace: Mat 5:40 puts a brother above the last garment you own.
A cloke for sin is usually a truth misapplied — liberty, providence, temperament — which is what makes it stick.
Nothing cloked is confessed, and nothing unconfessed is forgiven; Pro 28:13 makes uncovering the way to mercy.

etymology: From the Latin ornamentum, from ornare, “to adorn or furnish” — that which is added to a thing to set it off; in Scripture the word is turned inward, and the great ornament is one that cannot be put on.
biblical_def: An ornament is a thing added for beauty — the chain, the earring, the bracelet, the crown. Scripture treats ornaments with a striking evenhandedness. It does not forbid them: the LORD Himself decks Jerusalem with them in Ezekiel’s parable (Eze 16:11), Rebekah receives bracelets at the well, and Solomon likens a wise reprover on an obedient ear to “an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold” (Pro 25:12). Nor does it flatter them. When Israel sinned at Sinai the LORD commanded, “put off thy ornaments from thee, that I may know what to do unto thee” (Exo 33:5), and the mourning people wore none. Jeremiah’s complaint is that a maid can remember her ornaments better than Israel can remember her God. But the decisive word is Peter’s, and it does not abolish adorning — it relocates it. “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; but let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price” (1Pe 3:3-4). The contrast is not gold against plainness but corruptible against incorruptible, seen against hidden, priced by men against priced by God. Wisdom too is an ornament of grace unto the head (Pro 1:9).
webster_summary: That which is added to embellish; in Scripture chiefly the jewels and attire of a woman, set against the incorruptible ornament of a meek and quiet spirit.
webster_full: ORNAMENT, n. [L. ornamentum, from orno, to adorn, to furnish.] That which embellishes; something which, added to another thing, renders it more beautiful to the eye.
Hence, whatever confers honour or credit — an ornament to his profession, an ornament to the church.
In Scripture, the jewels, chains, bracelets, and attire worn upon the person (Eze 16:11; Isa 3:18-21).
Israel was commanded to put off her ornaments in the day of mourning after the golden calf (Exo 33:5-6).
The apostle sets the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit above all outward adorning (1Pe 3:3-4).
scriptures: Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Pro 1:9
For they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck.
Exo 33:5

For the LORD had said unto Moses, Say unto the children of Israel, Ye are a stiffnecked people: I will come up into the midst of thee in a moment, and consume thee: therefore now put off thy ornaments from thee, that I may know what to do unto thee.
corruption_summary: 1Pe 3:3-4 is corrupted from two sides: an outward legalism that reads it as a dress code and misses the heart, and a modern reading that treats the meek and quiet spirit as an outdated demand imposed on women.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is old and churchly. Whole communions have read 1Pe 3:3 as a rule about gold and hairstyles, measured obedience by jewellery, and produced congregations of plain-dressed women with proud hearts — which is exactly the outcome the text was written to prevent. The grammar refuses the reading: Peter’s let it not be is comparative, for the same construction would forbid the putting on of apparel altogether if pressed. His point is where the adorning lives, not what it costs. The second corruption is newer and runs the other way. A meek and quiet spirit is now widely presented as an antique expectation laid upon women to keep them silent and pliant, and the verse is either explained away or resented. But meekness in Scripture is nothing of the kind. It is the strength of the Lord Jesus, who was meek and lowly in heart and drove the traders from the temple; it is Moses’s character, the man who faced Pharaoh. Meekness is power under God’s government, and the promise attached to it is not obscurity but the earth.

Recover the pricing. Peter’s clause is in the sight of God of great price, and that clause is the whole argument. Every ornament is a bid for a verdict from somebody: the woman decking herself for the room, the man dressing for the office, all of it a case laid before an audience whose approval fades by evening. Peter does not say the bid is beneath a Christian; he says it is aimed too low. There is a valuation that never moves, made by One who sees the hidden man of the heart, and He has published His price list — the meek and quiet spirit is great in His sight. So the ornament question is a question of court. Dress for the room and you will be re-priced every season by people who will forget you. Dress the hidden man and you are already wearing what God calls costly, and it is incorruptible, and it goes into the grave and comes out again.
roots_summary: That which is added for beauty — permitted, stripped in mourning, and finally relocated by Peter to the hidden man of the heart.
roots_lines: Ornament — Latin ornamentum, from ornare, to adorn or furnish.
Hebrew 'adi, ornament or trappings (Exo 33:5; Eze 16:11); livyah, a wreath, in Pro 1:9.
Greek kosmos in 1Pe 3:3 — the same word rendered world, meaning ordered arrangement.
Exo 33:5-6 — the ornaments stripped off from Horeb onward as a token of national mourning.
1Pe 3:4 sets the incorruptible ornament against the corruptible, and God’s pricing against the room’s.
usage: Peter relocates adorning rather than abolishing it: the question is where the beauty lives, not what it cost.
Meekness is not timidity but strength under God’s government — Moses before Pharaoh, Christ in the temple.
Every ornament seeks a verdict from some court; the only court that never revises its pricing is God’s.

etymology: From the Saxon byndel, from bindan, “to bind” — a number of things bound together into one, so that what befalls the bundle befalls every thing in it.
biblical_def: A bundle is a number of separate things bound into one, so that they are carried, kept, or destroyed together. The word runs through Scripture as a figure of shared destiny. Joseph’s brethren empty their sacks and find every man’s bundle of money returned, and the whole company is afraid together (Gen 42:35). Paul gathers a bundle of sticks on Melita and a viper comes out of the heat (Act 28:3). The bride calls her beloved “a bundle of myrrh” that lies all night betwixt her breasts (Son 1:13) — the fragrance bound close and kept through the darkness. And in the parable of the tares, the harvest sorts the field into two bundles and only two: “Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn” (Mat 13:30). Nothing is left loose at the end. But the sweetest use is Abigail’s, when she tells the hunted David that his soul shall be bound in the bundle of life with the LORD his God, while the souls of his enemies are slung out as from the pocket of a sling. To be in that bundle is to be kept because of the company you are bound with, which is the whole doctrine of union with Christ and the perseverance of the saints in a single homely picture.
webster_summary: A number of things bound together; hence a company or collection sharing one fate, as the bundle of life and the bundles of tares.
webster_full: BUNDLE, n. [Sax. byndel, from bindan, to bind.] A number of things bound together; a package; a roll.
Anything bound or rolled into a convenient form for carriage or keeping.
In 1Sa 25:29, the bundle of life — the treasure-bag in which precious things are bound up for safe keeping.
In Mat 13:30, the tares are bound in bundles to be burned, the wheat gathered into the barn.
A bundle of myrrh (Son 1:13); a bundle of money (Gen 42:35); a bundle of sticks (Act 28:3).
scriptures: Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.
Son 1:13
A bundle of myrrh is my wellbeloved unto me; he shall lie all night betwixt my breasts.
And it came to pass as they emptied their sacks, that, behold, every man's bundle of money was in his sack: and when both they and their father saw the bundles of money, they were afraid.
Act 28:3
And when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks, and laid them on the fire, there came a viper out of the heat, and fastened on his hand.
corruption_summary: No modern movement disputes the word; what is commonly missed is that Abigail’s bundle of life is a doctrine of preservation, not a sentiment for gravestones.
corruption_paragraphs: “Bound in the bundle of life” has become a funeral inscription and little else, cut on stones by people who take it to mean something warm and vague about remembrance. Abigail meant something exact and she meant it about a living man. David was hunted; Saul was on the hills; Abigail was standing in a ravine with loaves and figs, talking a future king out of a slaughter he would have regretted all his days. Her comfort is that the LORD keeps David’s soul as a man keeps his valuables — bound up in the bag he carries himself, in the same bundle with his own treasure — and that the enemy’s soul, by contrast, is the stone in the sling, flung out and gone. It is a doctrine of keeping under fire, spoken to a man in the field, not a comfort reserved for the grave.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the bundle keeps what could not keep itself. A coin bound in a bag is not preserved by being a good coin; it is preserved by being in the bag, and by the strength of the hand that carries it. That is why Abigail’s figure says with the LORD thy God — the saint is bound in the same bundle as his God, and what would come at him must first come at Him. The New Testament says the same thing without the metaphor: your life is hid with Christ in God, and none shall pluck them out of My Father’s hand. And Mat 13:30 supplies the sober other half. Everyone is bound into some bundle at the harvest, tares as surely as wheat, and the binding is done by reapers who make no mistakes. The only question that matters is which bundle, and the answer is settled now, in the field, while both are still growing together.
roots_summary: Things bound into one so that they share a fate — the bundle of life that keeps the saint, and the bundles of tares bound for burning.
roots_lines: Bundle — Saxon byndel, from bindan, to bind.
Hebrew tseror, a bag or pouch in which valuables are bound up (1Sa 25:29; Son 1:13).
Greek desme in Mat 13:30, a sheaf or faggot bound for the fire.
Abigail’s figure sets the bound treasure against the slung stone — kept, or cast away.
The harvest of Mat 13 leaves nothing loose: every stalk is bound into one bundle or the other.
usage: 1Sa 25:29 is a doctrine of preservation spoken to a hunted man, not an epitaph for a stone.
The coin is kept by the bag and the hand that carries it, never by its own worth.
At the harvest nothing is left loose — tares are bound as carefully as wheat is gathered.

etymology: Through the Old French ivurie from the Latin ebur, elephant tooth — the hard white substance of the tusk, brought to Israel by the navy of Tharshish and prized above almost every material for its whiteness and its cost.
biblical_def: Ivory is the dense white substance of the elephant’s tusk, imported into Israel by sea and reckoned among the costliest of materials. Scripture uses it two ways, and they stand at opposite ends of the moral world. In the Song and the Psalms it is beauty: the beloved’s body as bright ivory overlaid with sapphires, the bride’s neck as a tower of ivory, and the King’s garments smelling of myrrh and aloes and cassia “out of the ivory palaces, whereby they have made thee glad” (Psa 45:8) — a messianic psalm, where the ivory is the splendour of the Bridegroom’s own house. Solomon’s great throne of ivory overlaid with the best gold belongs here too, the glory of a kingdom at peace. But ivory turns. Ahab built an ivory house (1Ki 22:39), and the historian sets that single fact beside a reign of Baal-worship and Naboth’s stolen vineyard, so that the panelling and the murder stand in one sentence. Amos then pronounces sentence: “the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall have an end, saith the LORD” (Amo 3:15). His indictment is not luxury alone but luxury asleep — men who “lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches” while the ruin of Joseph goes unlamented (Amo 6:4-6).
webster_summary: The hard white substance of the elephant’s tusk; in Scripture the splendour of Solomon’s throne and the Bridegroom’s palaces, and the emblem of Samaria’s luxury under judgment.
webster_full: IVORY, n. [Fr. ivoire; L. ebur, the tooth of an elephant.] The tusk of the elephant, a hard, solid, firm substance, of a fine white colour, susceptible of a high polish.
It was brought to Palestine by the navy of Tharshish, with gold, silver, apes, and peacocks (1Ki 10:22).
Used for thrones, beds, couches, panelling, benches, and vessels (1Ki 10:18; Amo 6:4; Eze 27:6; Rev 18:12).
An ivory house is one wainscotted or inlaid with ivory, as Ahab’s (1Ki 22:39) and those of Samaria (Amo 3:15).
Figuratively, whiteness and smoothness of surpassing beauty (Son 5:14; 7:4).
scriptures: Now the rest of the acts of Ahab, and all that he did, and the ivory house which he made, and all the cities that he built, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Amo 3:15
And I will smite the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall have an end, saith the LORD.
Amo 6:4
That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall;
Psa 45:8
All thy garments smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia, out of the ivory palaces, whereby they have made thee glad.
corruption_summary: Amos is quoted selectively at both extremes — enlisted as a manifesto against wealth as such, or dismissed by the comfortable as thundering about somebody else’s beds.
corruption_paragraphs: Amo 6:4 is a favourite text of preaching that treats prosperity itself as the crime, and on that reading Solomon’s ivory throne would be a sin and Psa 45’s ivory palaces a scandal. Amos says something more searching. Read the sentence to its end: they lie upon beds of ivory, they chant to the sound of the viol, they drink wine in bowls and anoint themselves with the chief ointments, “but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.” That last clause is the indictment. The sin is a couch so comfortable that the nation’s ruin cannot reach the man lying on it — wealth used as an anaesthetic against the things that ought to have broken his heart. The opposite error is just as common, and it belongs to those who are comfortable: Amos is read as a period piece about eighth-century Samaria, or as a rebuke aimed at somebody richer, always somebody richer, and so the couch stays exactly where it is.

Ahab’s house makes the same point in narrative. The chronicler mentions the ivory house in one breath with the record of a reign, and the reader who knows the previous chapters knows what stood in the walls: Jezebel’s prophets fed at the queen’s table, the vineyard of a murdered man, a kingdom taught to worship Baal. Ivory panelling is not sin; ivory panelling paid for by Naboth’s blood, in a house that hunted Elijah, is the exact shape of what God overthrows. Amos promises that the winter house and the summer house go down together, and Revelation closes the account, listing vessels of ivory in the cargo of a city that falls in a single hour. So the word puts one question to a comfortable man, and it is not how much do you own but what can still reach you. If the affliction of Joseph can no longer get through the panelling, the panelling is already under sentence.
roots_summary: The white tusk of the elephant — Solomon’s throne and the Bridegroom’s palaces on one hand, Ahab’s house and Samaria’s couches on the other.
roots_lines: Ivory — Old French ivurie, Latin ebur, the elephant’s tooth.
Hebrew shen, a tooth, alone or with habbim (elephants) in 1Ki 10:22.
Imported by the navy of Tharshish once in three years with gold, apes, and peacocks.
Ahab’s ivory house (1Ki 22:39) stands in the record beside Baal and Naboth’s vineyard.
Amo 3:15 and 6:4 sentence the ivory houses and the ivory beds; Rev 18:12 lists ivory in Babylon’s last cargo.
usage: Psa 45:8 puts ivory palaces around the Bridegroom — the material itself is never the sin.
Amos condemns the couch that made a man unable to grieve for the affliction of Joseph.
The chronicler names Ahab’s ivory house and Naboth’s vineyard in the same record for a reason.
